name: Build a fire in wet conditions
blurb: The genuinely useful fire skill. Rain does not stop a fire; poor material selection does. The trick is knowing where dry wood hides after three days of drizzle.
gear: A knife or small axe for splitting
A candle stub or a commercial fire starter as insurance
steps: Find standing dead wood — never wood off the ground. Dead branches still attached to a tree stay drier than anything lying down.
Split everything. Wood is wet on the outside and dry at the core, so batoning a wrist-thick piece gives you dry heartwood.
Make feather sticks: fine curls shaved from dry inner wood, which light far more readily than shavings you have collected.
Look for natural dry tinder: birch bark, resinous fatwood from old stumps, dead conifer twigs from the underside of the canopy, the fluffy inner bark of dead standing trees.
Build a platform of split wood to keep the fire off wet ground, and lay a lean-to of graded kindling before lighting.
Light it low and shelter the flame with your body until the kindling is genuinely committed.
tips: Gather three times as much kindling as you think you need, then double it. Running out mid-build is the number one wet-fire failure.
Never lay a wet fire directly on soaked ground — steam from below will kill it.
proof: You start and sustain a fire after a full day of rain, using only what you gathered on site.
